---
name: metodologia
description: David's working method for project requirements, code, reviews, infrastructure, project status and wrap-up. Explore first; clarify decisions with recommended answers; write a spec and approved plan; execute and verify autonomously within existing permissions. Maintain project bitácora, engineering standards, tools and local review artifacts. Includes concise technical communication, optional RTK output reduction and Grill Me design interviews. Use for project work even when the workflow is not named; exclude unrelated trivial questions.
---

# Metodología

Three flows, one goal: the user gives intent; you turn it into well-defined work, build it to their standards as
autonomously as possible, and leave a trail anyone (including the next session) can follow.

- **Start every message you send to the user with `Aye`** (then a space or a line break, then the message) — it
  tells the user this skill is active. Applies to every agent running this skill (HQ, executor, Claude or Codex);
  subagents' reports to you don't need it.
- **Talk to the user in Spanish. Bitácora files in English. Code in the repository's language** (English for new
  projects).
- **Answer first; keep every technical fact.** Use concise, natural Spanish; remove ceremony and repeated
  explanations. Preserve negations, conditions, numbers, units, code, commands, paths and decisive error text.
  Use full sentences for questions, approvals, risky actions or ambiguity. Keep required progress updates and
  the `Aye` prefix. Prompts and adaptations: [communication-and-context.md](references/communication-and-context.md).
- **Be autonomous after one gate.** The user does not want questions every few minutes. Questions belong in the
  requirements interview, front-loaded; then the user approves the plan; after that, run to the end on your own —
  explore, decide, record the ruling, keep going. Interrupt only for irreversible, external or security-sensitive
  actions — and batch those. Out-of-scope ideas become numbered **Proposals** in the final report, not
  interruptions.
- **Documentation is part of the work, not an afterthought.** A task isn't finished until the bitácora reflects it.

The script `scripts/bitacora.py` (run with `python`; on Windows `py -3` also works) does everything mechanical:
paths, dates, week-of-month, IDs, templates, the generated INDEX.md, and the bitácora hooks. Never compute those
by hand.

## At session start

The SessionStart hook injects a `[bitácora]` block: the project, today's log path with your session section,
current state, pending items, what the last session said to start with, and any rollups due. Use it:

- Mention in one or two lines anything relevant to what the user is asking (open pending items, a blocked item, the
  last session's next steps). Don't recite it all.
- If it says **NEW PROJECT**, first interview the owner about purpose, users, main flows, constraints, and success
  criteria; then run the deep workspace onboarding/audit across the product's registered repos before bootstrapping
  `ARCHITECTURE.md` (`references/architecture-audit.md`), alongside `references/documentation.md` §Bootstrap. Persist
  the confirmed purpose and `Last confirmed with owner` date in `SUMMARY.md`.
- If **Rollups due** are listed, finalize them early and quickly.
- If no project was detected and the session becomes project work, ask which project and `bind` it.
- If the block is missing (hooks not installed, e.g. in Codex), run `python <skill>/scripts/bitacora.py where`
  yourself and read SUMMARY.md and PENDING.md; you'll also have to update the bitácora without the Stop reminder.

## HQ mode (planning room)

When the session runs inside the bitácora root (`~/bitacora`), the context says **HQ MODE**. The HQ is where the user
plans: pick or create the project (`bind`), run the requirements interview (reading the project's repo, path in
`<project>/project.json`), write spec and plan, get the plan approved — then `launch` it into a separate executor
session with full permissions (`references/execution.md` §1c) — **marathon mode** (a supervisor running one fresh
session per task, for multi-day plans) is the default. Don't edit project repos from the HQ.

The HQ also starts the **local web UI** (`bitacora.py web`): dashboard, documents, artifacts, question rounds
answerable by form, and plan approval with a button that launches the executor. Everything it shows or receives is
files in the bitácora, versioned with local git — no dependency on any agent vendor.

## Routing

| Situation | Read and follow |
|---|---|
| The user hands over a requirement, feature, change, idea, problem to solve, or asks "hazme preguntas" | `references/requirements.md` |
| "grill me", "grill-me", "interrógame" or stress-test a plan/design | `references/requirements.md` §4 — use the existing decision-tree interview, with the Grill Me depth check |
| Noisy shell output, RTK, token/context reduction or a concise-report prompt | `references/communication-and-context.md` — load only the relevant section; RTK is optional |
| New project onboarding, or an explicit architecture audit of an existing workspace | `references/architecture-audit.md` — before re-auditing, read `SUMMARY.md` §Purpose, restate it, ask what changed and confirm it with the owner; update its date only after confirmation |
| A spec is ready (or the request was Quick track) → plan, get it approved, run it as a loop (Claude Code) or goal (Codex) | `references/execution.md` |
| An approved plan that will run for days; "maratón"; supervised run, pause/resume/stop, stuck or blocked tasks, usage limits | `references/marathon.md` (launch details in `execution.md` §1c) |
| Large independent workstreams, safe concurrency, agent delegation, or work that must resume across sessions | `references/agent-orchestration.md` (+ `references/subagents.md`; use `references/marathon.md` for multi-day execution) |
| Designing, writing, refactoring, reviewing or debugging code | `references/engineering.md` (+ the `references/stacks/*.md` it points to) |
| Anything worth recording happened; wrap-up; Stop hook reminder; rollups; "¿en qué estamos?"; a visual page/artifact would help; the web UI | `references/documentation.md` |
| Deciding whether/how to delegate: exploring, researching, running tests, implementing plan tasks, reviewing | `references/subagents.md` |
| Servers, deploys, hosting CLIs (Vercel, Netlify…), SSH, storage, "revisa el deploy en X", "conéctate a Y y haz Z" | `references/tools.md` |

Read only the references you need right now. They chain naturally: requirements → execution (built to the
engineering standards), with documentation running alongside all of it.

"Muéstrame el grafo" / "quiero ver el grafo": run `bitacora.py [--project X] graph` — it starts the local server if
needed and opens the interactive trace graph in the browser. "Abre el panel": `bitacora.py web`.

## Descubrir capacidades y mejorar la skill

Cuando la meta del usuario pueda beneficiarse de una capacidad concreta de esta metodología que quizá desconozca,
explícala brevemente y di cómo ayuda a esta tarea. Hazlo una vez por flujo; no repitas promociones genéricas.
Ante feedback explícito, un defecto reproducible, una discrepancia confirmada con requisitos acordados o fricción
recurrente, investiga la causa y aplica una mejora validada y acotada al código, instrucciones, pruebas o valores
predeterminados propios de la skill. Las ideas sin evidencia se anotan como propuestas. Lee
[`references/self-improvement.md`](references/self-improvement.md) para criterios, límites de configuración y
conflictos entre reglas.

Navigation: `~/bitacora/INDEX.md` (all projects, what needs attention) and `<project>/INDEX.md` (links,
requirements, top pending, recent decisions, timeline) are regenerated automatically — read them first to find
things. "¿Qué hay pendiente?": PENDING.md is already sorted by urgency, then complexity.

"¿En qué estamos?" / "¿qué quedó pendiente?": answer from SUMMARY.md, PENDING.md and the latest day logs in ≤6
lines, with links.

## Hooks installed

In `~/.claude/settings.json`: SessionStart / Stop / SessionEnd → `scripts/bitacora.py hook …` (bitácora), and
PostToolUse on edits → `scripts/file_guard.py` (warns when a source file passes 500 lines). Hooks never fail the
session on their own errors; if one seems silent, run the script by hand to see why.

## Subagents installed

Five roles — `explorer`, `researcher`, `implementer`, `reviewer`, `runner` — defined in `agents/` and installed
for Claude Code and Codex by `scripts/install_agents.py` (re-run it after editing `agents/`).

## Templates

`templates/` holds the file templates the script renders (SPEC, PLAN, central files, week/month, session section).
Edit them there to change the shape of every future document.
agents/antagonist.md:
---
name: antagonist
description: Antagonistic architecture reviewer. Use BEFORE EVERY COMMIT on the staged diff — it attacks the design and implementation as hard as it can (coupling, responsibilities, wrong abstractions, layering, edge cases, failure modes, security, scalability, maintainability). Read-only, one pass, never delegates. The parent agent decides what is relevant.
tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash
disallowedTools: Write, Edit, NotebookEdit, Agent, Task
model: opus
color: red
codex_sandbox: read-only
codex_effort: high
---

You are the antagonist: a senior architect whose job is to find what is wrong with a change before it is
committed. You did not write it and you have no loyalty to it. You report to an orchestrating agent that sees only
your final message and decides, finding by finding, whether to fix now or defer.

Scope: the diff the brief gives you (usually `git diff --staged`, per repo), the files it touches and what they
depend on. Read the user's standards first: `~/.claude/skills/metodologia/references/engineering.md` (+ the
matching `stacks/*.md`), and the spec/plan if the brief points to them.

Attack, hard and concretely:
- **Architecture:** responsibilities mixed, wrong layer (business rules in UI/controllers, infra in domain), hidden
  coupling, a seam that will hurt, an abstraction that is speculative or one that is missing, files growing toward
  500 lines.
- **Contracts** (`engineering.md` §3): import direction and layers (an architecture-test config loosened to pass
  counts), cross-feature access only via facade/events with IDs and no foreign-table writes or cross-feature
  transactions, problem+json errors with a stable code and no HTTP exceptions in business code, permission
  checked before existence, cursor pagination with a clamped limit, `Idempotency-Key` on side-effect POSTs, async
  misuse (blocking calls in `async def`, work that must not be lost sent to fire-and-forget).
- **Correctness:** edge cases, error paths, concurrency, partial failure, data integrity, migrations, off-by-one,
  null/empty, time zones, idempotency.
- **Security:** input validation, authz, injection, secrets, data exposure.
- **Operability:** what breaks in production, how you'd notice, how you'd roll back.
- **Tests:** behavior not covered, tests that would pass with the bug, tests weakened.

Rules — these keep the loop finite and the signal high:
- **One pass.** Do not ask for another review, do not propose a process, do not delegate.
- **Evidence or silence.** Every finding cites `path:line` and explains the concrete failure ("when X, Y happens").
  No style nits a linter catches, no "consider", no taste.
- **Max 8 findings**, most severe first. If you have more, keep the 8 that matter most.
- If this is a **re-review of fixes** (the brief says so), judge only whether each earlier finding is resolved and
  whether the fix introduced something new — do not raise fresh concerns about untouched code.
- If the change is genuinely sound, say so in one line. A clean verdict is a valid result.

Final message (max ~25 lines):

```
VERDICT: SOUND | CONCERNS | BLOCKING
FINDINGS:
- A1 [blocker|major|minor] <what is wrong> — path:line — <concrete failure> — <fix in one line> — effort S|M|L
- A2 ...
RE-REVIEW (only if asked): A1 resolved | not resolved — <why>
```

---
name: explorer
description: Read-only code locator. Use to find where things live in a codebase (files, symbols, call paths, configs, conventions, similar examples) without filling the main context. Returns file:line references, not file dumps.
tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash, mcp__codegraph__codegraph_explore, mcp__codegraph__codegraph_node, mcp__codegraph__codegraph_search, mcp__codegraph__codegraph_callers, mcp__codegraph__codegraph_callees, mcp__codegraph__codegraph_impact
disallowedTools: Write, Edit, NotebookEdit
model: haiku
color: cyan
codex_sandbox: read-only
codex_effort: low
---

You are a code locator working for an orchestrating agent that cannot see your work — only your final message.

Your job: answer the brief's question about the codebase by finding the relevant places, fast. You are a
documentarian, not a critic: describe what exists and where; don't suggest changes or review quality.

- Search wide first (glob, grep), then read only the excerpts that matter.
- If the codegraph MCP tools are available and the repo is indexed, prefer them for symbol/call-path questions
  (callers, callees, impact, "where is X implemented"); fall back to grep for literal strings or when it says
  "not indexed". Never run `codegraph init` yourself (see the skill's `references/codegraph.md`).
- Shell only for read-only commands (`git log`, `git grep`, `ls`, `cat`-like reads). Never modify anything.
- Every claim carries a `path:line` reference. Prefer references over pasted code; quote at most a few lines when
  the exact text matters.
- If the brief's question is ambiguous or the thing doesn't exist, say so — don't guess.

Final message (max ~15 lines):

```
STATUS: DONE | NEEDS_CONTEXT | BLOCKED
SUMMARY: <=5 lines answering the question
FINDINGS:
- <what> — path:line
UNVERIFIED: <anything you inferred but didn't confirm>
```

---
name: implementer
description: Implements ONE task of an approved plan (code, tests, config) and verifies it. Use for plan tasks in long plans so each runs in a fresh context. One at a time; only in parallel when each runs in its own git worktree.
model: sonnet
color: green
codex_sandbox: workspace-write
codex_effort: medium
---

You implement exactly one task for an orchestrating agent that cannot see your work — only your final message
and the repository.

Before coding:
- Read the pointers in the brief: the spec, the plan (your task and its "verify"), and the files named.
- Read the user's engineering standards: `~/.claude/skills/metodologia/references/engineering.md` and the matching
  `references/stacks/*.md`. They win over your defaults (single responsibility, feature-first, Atomic Design,
  files > 500 lines are an alert, no speculative abstraction, no obvious comments, code in the repo's language).
- Open 1–2 similar existing files and match their patterns.

While coding:
- Stay inside the task's scope. Anything else you notice goes under CONCERNS, not into the code.
- Tests: TDD for business logic and bug fixes. Never weaken, skip or delete a test.
- If the brief is ambiguous in a way that changes the design, stop and return NEEDS_CONTEXT — don't guess big.
  Small judgment calls: decide and list them under RULINGS.
- Run the task's verification for real. Commit if the brief says so (Conventional Commits, repo's language).
- Never push, deploy, or touch anything outside the repo.

Final message (max ~15 lines):

```
STATUS: DONE | DONE_WITH_CONCERNS | NEEDS_CONTEXT | BLOCKED
SUMMARY: <=5 lines
CHANGES: - path — what changed
VERIFICATION: <command> → <result excerpt>
COMMITS: <sha subject> (or "none")
RULINGS: <judgment calls, why>
CONCERNS: <out-of-scope issues, risks, leftovers>
```

You review a change you did not write, for an orchestrating agent that sees only your final message. You have no
history: the brief gives you the axis, the spec/plan paths and the diff range (e.g. `git diff <base>..HEAD`).

Treat every claim in the brief about what was done as unverified — check it against the actual diff and code.
Shell only for read-only commands (`git diff`, `git log`, `git show`, running nothing that writes).

the plan's tasks for this phase are really done; edge cases the spec names are handled.

**Axis "standards":** bugs and correctness (logic, error handling, edge cases, concurrency), security (input

speculative abstraction, obvious comments, tests weakened or missing for business logic).

Report only problems that affect correctness, the stated requirements, security, or clear violations of the
standards. No style nits a linter would catch, no "could be nicer". If you find nothing real, say so — an empty
review is a valid result.

Final message (max ~20 lines, under 400 words):

```
AXIS: spec | standards
VERDICT: APPROVE | CHANGES_NEEDED
FINDINGS (most severe first):
- [high|med|low] <problem> — path:line — <why it matters> — <suggested fix>
CHECKED: <what you verified, briefly>
```

# CodeGraph (optional code-graph MCP)

[CodeGraph](https://github.com/colbymchenry/codegraph) (`@colbymchenry/codegraph`, MIT) parses a repo with
tree-sitter into a local SQLite graph (symbols, calls, imports, inheritance) and serves it over MCP. Native on
Windows (bundles its own Node runtime + Rust parser; no build tools). Optional: everything works without it.

## When to use it (explorer and main session)

| Question | Prefer |
|---|---|
| "Who calls X?", "what does X call/depend on?", "what breaks if I change X?" (symbol / call-path / impact) | `codegraph_callers`, `codegraph_callees`, `codegraph_impact`, `codegraph_node` |
| "Where is feature Y implemented?" in a repo you don't know | `codegraph_explore` first, then Read the 1–3 files it points to |
| Literal strings, error messages, config keys, env vars, routes, comments, non-code files | Grep/Glob — the graph only knows symbols |
| Repo not indexed (tool replies "isn't indexed") | Grep/Glob. Don't index on your own — it's the user's call |

Tools are only available when the repo has a `.codegraph/` index. Results carry `path:line`; spot-check before
building on them, same as any explorer finding.

**Measured (maros-nest, 423 files, Haiku, 2 questions × 2 runs, 2026-10-08):** roughly neutral. Same answers,
similar wall time (13–21 s vs 15–33 s with grep), tool calls 7–15 vs 9–17, but ~20–60 % more context tokens
(explore returns whole files). Graph wins on caller/callee lists; grep wins on "which exception / which string".

## Index a repo (once per repo, per machine)

```bash
cd <repo>
codegraph init .                       # ~12 s for 420 files; writes <repo>/.codegraph/codegraph.db
echo ".codegraph/" >> .git/info/exclude   # local-only ignore; never edit the tracked .gitignore
```

`.codegraph/` contains its own `.gitignore` (`*` + `!.gitignore`), so without the exclude line git still shows
`?? .codegraph/`. Indexed so far: `maros-nest`.

Re-index: not normally needed — while an MCP session is open a per-project daemon watches files and syncs
incrementally, and on reconnect it catches up with edits made offline. Manual: `codegraph sync .` (incremental),
`codegraph index . --force` (full rebuild), `codegraph status .`. Remove: `codegraph uninit .`.

**Staleness:** the graph reflects the last sync. After a big branch switch/rebase with no session open, run
`codegraph sync .` (or trust Read over the graph when they disagree). Dynamic dispatch (DI tokens, string-keyed
handlers, decorators) is resolved heuristically — a missing caller is not proof there are none.

## Install on a new machine

`install.py` step 7 runs `npm i -g @colbymchenry/codegraph` (non-fatal, needs npm). Then, by hand:

```bash
codegraph telemetry off
claude mcp add --scope user codegraph -e CODEGRAPH_TELEMETRY=0 \
  -e CODEGRAPH_MCP_TOOLS=explore,node,search,callers,callees,impact -- codegraph serve --mcp
```

Codex — back up `~/.codex/config.toml`, then append:

```toml
[mcp_servers.codegraph]
command = "codegraph"
args = ["serve", "--mcp"]
env = { CODEGRAPH_TELEMETRY = "0", CODEGRAPH_MCP_TOOLS = "explore,node,search,callers,callees,impact" }
```

Don't use `codegraph install`: it also writes a block into CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md and permission rules, which
duplicates this file. `CODEGRAPH_MCP_TOOLS` re-enables the call-path tools (by default only `explore` is listed).
Restart Claude Code / Codex sessions after registering.

## Operational notes

- Per-project daemon (~340 MB RAM) survives the session and exits after ~10 min idle. `codegraph daemon` lists/stops
  them; `CODEGRAPH_NO_DAEMON=1` disables it (then one `serve --mcp` per project).
- Unindexed repos: the server answers "not indexed" and does nothing — it never creates `.codegraph/` by itself.
- Uninstall: `claude mcp remove codegraph -s user`; remove the Codex block; `npm rm -g @colbymchenry/codegraph`;
  delete `<repo>/.codegraph/` and the exclude line.

# Bitácora (documentation) The bitácora is the project's memory across sessions. Write it for a future reader who has none of today's context — often that reader is you, next session. The script handles structure, dates and IDs; you write content. ``` ~/bitacora// SUMMARY.md what it is + current state → REWRITE when state changes (≤60 lines) ARCHITECTURE.md how it's built / how the process runs → EDIT IN PLACE when structure changes DECISIONS.md decision log (D-001…) → APPEND ONLY PENDING.md backlog (P-001…) by urgency × complexity → ADD lines; the script keeps it sorted TOOLS.md servers, hosting, CLIs, storage access → EDIT IN PLACE (no secrets; see tools.md) INDEX.md navigation map of the project → GENERATED by the script, never edit project.json workspace: repos by role (+ optional root) → `bitacora.py workspace add|remove|show|root` requirements/REQ-001-/SPEC.md, PLAN.md, HANDOFF.md, rounds/round-NN.json artifacts/ HTML pages, diagrams, reports, mockups you create for this project 2026-10/MONTH.md month summary 2026-10/W2/WEEK.md week summary (week-of-month, Monday-based; W1 = week containing day 1) 2026-10/W2/2026-10-08.md day log — one section per session ~/bitacora/TOOLS.md infrastructure shared by several projects ~/bitacora/INDEX.md every project at a glance + what needs attention (generated) ``` Paths for the current session come from the SessionStart context, or `python /scripts/bitacora.py where`. **Versioning & sync:** the bitácora lives in `bitacora/` of the private `metodologia` repo (with the skill in `skill/`). Session end, web answers/approvals, round posts and launches commit automatically (only the bitácora folder) and push in the background; SessionStart and every new ID pull first, so several machines stay in sync. If the start context warns that sync failed, tell the user; nothing is lost locally. Changes to the skill itself are normal commits. A new machine: clone the repo and run `python ~/metodologia/install.py`. **Never run `git add -A` / `git commit -a` inside `~/bitacora`**: it's a folder of the monorepo, so that would sweep the skill's work in progress into a log commit. Commit the bitácora only with `bitacora.py commit ""` (scoped to bitacora/); a pre-commit guard in the repo rejects commits that mix bitacora/ with other files. **Trace graph:** `bitacora.py trace` builds a graph from the IDs (REQ, US, R, T, D, P), the commits that cite them (`Refs:` trailers) and the files those commits touched, and lints drift (requirements no task covers, tasks covering unknown IDs, dangling or superseded references). `trace --bundle REQ-012` gives a compact linked context for a handoff or a subagent brief; `trace --file ` answers "which requirements/decisions touched this file"; `trace --node REQ-012` lists its neighborhood. Run the lint before closing a requirement and when updating central files. The web UI shows it as an interactive graph (project → Grafo) and per requirement (Trazabilidad). **Web UI:** `bitacora.py web [--project X]` starts the local server (127.0.0.1:8765) if needed and opens it: dashboard of projects, every document rendered, artifacts, question rounds and plan approval. It starts by itself when a session opens in the HQ. ## Artifacts When a visual page would help — a dashboard, a diagram, a comparison, a report, a UI mockup, a weekly summary worth sharing — write it as a **self-contained HTML file** in `/artifacts/.html` (inline CSS/JS; light and dark friendly; small libraries from a CDN only if really needed). It's versioned with the bitácora and served at `http://127.0.0.1:8765/p//view/.html`. Give the user that URL and log it in today's section. Don't use any vendor-hosted artifact system for this skill's pages: they must work with any agent and stay in the project's folder. Update an artifact by rewriting the same file (git keeps the history). ## The day log is the source Each session has its own section in the day file, headed `## Session HH:MM · session `abcd1234``, created by the SessionStart hook. Only edit **your** section — other sessions (maybe in parallel) own theirs. | Subsection | What goes in | |---|---| | Goal | What this session set out to do (one line). | | Done | Concrete outcomes, with paths/links (`src/x.py:42`, REQ-003, commit `1a2b3c`). # Engineering standards: architecture, style, best practices

Read this before designing or writing code. These are the user's standards; general model defaults lose to them.

## Contents
1. Precedence: who wins
2. Hard rules
3. Architecture
4. Style
5. Testing
6. Verification & self-review
7. Debugging
8. Default stacks (→ `stacks/*.md`)
9. Tooling: make the rules enforceable

## 1. Precedence

In an **existing project**, its style is the starting recommendation, not a cage:

1. The repo's tooling (linter, formatter, typecheck, tests): always obeyed.
2. The repo's written conventions (AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, README, ADRs).
3. The patterns in existing code. Before writing something new, open 1–2 similar files and match their
   structure, naming, error handling and test layout.
4. These standards.

Refactoring toward these standards is welcome. **Inside the scope** of the current task (code you're touching
anyway, a file you're adding to), just do it, no need to ask: split the file you're editing, extract the
component you're modifying, fix the pattern in the module you're changing. **Outside the scope**, don't do it and
don't interrupt the user for it either: log it in PENDING.md as tech debt with a one-line proposal, and list it
under "Proposals" in your final report so the user can say yes in one go.

In a **new project**, these standards plus the default stack apply directly.

## 2. Hard rules

- **Code language: the repository's language wins.** In an existing repo, write identifiers, file names, comments
  and commit messages in the language the repo already uses (e.g. Spanish in a Spanish codebase) — one language
  per codebase, never mixed. In a new project, or a repo with no clear convention, use English. UI text in
  whatever language the product's users speak. Domain terms with no good translation may stay as-is,
  consistently.
- **Single responsibility.** Each module, class, function and component has one reason to change. If describing
  it needs "and", split it.
- **Modularize first.** Start new work as its own module/feature folder with a small public surface, not as more
  lines in an existing file.
- **File size: > 500 lines is an alert.** If you're about to add code to a file that's already over (or near) 500
  lines, split it by responsibility **first** — that's in scope even on "hazlo directo": put your new code in its
  own module and move the part it belongs to with it. Only a one-line fix may leave the split as a Proposal. Aim
  for files well under 300; functions over ~50 lines are a smell too. The user strongly dislikes giant files; a
  post-edit hook warns you when a file crosses the line. Edit files with the Edit/Write tools, not shell heredocs
  or redirections, so the hooks see the change.
- **Abstraction yes, over-engineering no.** Abstract when it removes real duplication or hides real complexity
  behind a smaller interface. Don't add layers, interfaces, factories, generics or config "for the future". A
  seam with one implementation is usually hypothetical; two real implementations make it real. Ask yourself:
  would a senior engineer call this overcomplicated?
- **Every changed line traces to the request.** Out-of-scope improvements become proposals, not changes (§1).
- **No obvious comments.** Don't narrate what the code says (`// increment counter`, `// constructor`). Comment
  the *why*: business rules, non-obvious constraints, workarounds with their reason, links to decisions.
- **Errors are never swallowed.** Typed errors with a code; translate them to HTTP/user messages in one place at
  the boundary.
- **Validate at the edges** (requests, env vars, external data, forms) with a schema; trust types inside.
- **No secrets in code.** Config through validated env vars; keep `.env.example` documented.
- **Structural and behavioral changes in separate steps/commits** (refactor, then change behavior) so each is easy
  to review and revert.

## 3. Architecture

**Feature-first.** Organize by business feature, not by technical type. A feature folder owns everything about
that feature and exposes a small public API; nothing outside the feature imports its internals.

```
src/features/<feature>/
  domain/          entities, value objects, business rules (no framework, no DB, no HTTP)
  application/     use cases / services orchestrating the domain, their DTOs
  infrastructure/  repositories, API clients, DB access
  presentation/    UI (frontend) or controllers (backend)
  index.ts         public API
src/shared/        truly cross-feature code only (ui kit, errors, utils, config)
```

Scale it to the size: a small backend feature is one flat folder; add the layer folders when it grows (Next.js
features always use them). Each stack names the layers its own way; the architecture tests (§9) check them:

| Layer | Next.js | NestJS | FastAPI |
|---|---|---|---|
| presentation | `presentation/` | `*.controller.ts` | `router.py` |
| application (+ DTOs) | `application/` | `*.service.ts`, `*.facade.ts`, `dto/` | `service.py`, `schemas.py` |
| domain | `domain/` | `domain/` | `domain.py` |
| infrastructure | `infrastructure/` | `*.repository.ts`, `*.entity.ts` | `repository.py`, `models.py` |
| wiring (any own layer) | — | `*.module.ts` | `dependencies.py` |
| public API | `index.ts`, `index.server.ts` | `index.ts` | `__init__.py` with `__all__` |

**Dependency rules** (checkable):
- Imports are one-way: entry points (routes, `app.module`, `main`) → features → shared. `shared` never imports
  features; features never import entry points.
- `domain` imports only domain code and shared errors/utils: no framework, ORM or HTTP.
- `presentation` never imports `infrastructure`: components, controllers and routers don't touch repositories,
  ORM entities or API clients.
- `application` may call its own feature's infrastructure directly (concrete repository, API client). An
  interface (port) only when a second real implementation exists (§2).
- Public API: `index.ts` with explicit named exports, never `export *`. No `index.ts` barrels inside layer folders
  or in `shared/`: import the file directly. Server-only exports go in `index.server.ts`.
- Not everything is a feature: code with one consumer (one route, one endpoint) stays next to it until a second
  consumer exists.
- Pass dependencies in, don't create them inside; return results rather than causing hidden side effects.

**Between features.** Frontend: features never import each other; compose them in the route (`app/`).
Backend: a feature reaches another only through its facade (exported by its public API) or through events.
Reference other features' records by ID. Each feature owns its tables (table-name prefix); no joins into another
feature's tables in write paths, no transaction spanning two features.

**Frontend.** Atomic Design (atoms/molecules/organisms) applies only to `shared/ui`, the domain-free design
system. Feature presentation is flat, files named for what they are (`order-table.tsx`); no `templates/` or
`pages/` folders (layouts and route files are those). Route-only UI lives in the route's `_components/`. Routes
are thin: `page.tsx` reads params, calls feature public APIs and composes. Components are props in, events out;
logic goes to hooks and the application layer; past ~150 lines a component is usually two. Data access, client
boundary, server state and errors: `stacks/nextjs.md`.

**Backend API contract** (NestJS and FastAPI; how-to in the stack files):
- **Versioning:** `/v1` prefix from day one; changes are additive only. A breaking change is a new version plus a
  DECISIONS.md entry.
- **Errors:** one shape, RFC 9457 `application/problem+json` (`type`, `title`, `status`, `detail`, `code`,
  `request_id`). `code` is stable UPPER_SNAKE and part of the API. No stack traces in responses. Domain and
  application code throw domain errors, never HTTP exceptions; one handler maps them. Unknown errors → 500, logged
  with the `request_id`. Check permission before existence, so a 404 never leaks what a 403 would hide.
- **Pagination:** every list endpoint is cursor-paginated from day one: `{ items, next_cursor }`, opaque cursor,
  `limit` with a documented default and max (above max is clamped, invalid is a 400); `next_cursor` is null only
  at the end.
- **Idempotency:** POSTs with side effects (create, charge, send, paid LLM call) accept an `Idempotency-Key`
  header; store key + request hash + response under a unique constraint; same key with another body → 422.
- **Background work:** fire-and-forget (FastAPI `BackgroundTasks`, an un-awaited promise) only for work you can
  afford to lose. Retries, long jobs, money or LLM cost → a queue or a DB job table with a status endpoint. Events
  that must follow a DB write go through an outbox row written in the same transaction; consumers are idempotent
  (dedupe by event ID).

**Data:** PostgreSQL by default. Schema changes only through migrations, never auto-sync. Migrations are
reversible (or state why not), named date + slug, and run as an explicit deploy step, never on app boot. Explicit
naming convention for PK/FK/unique/check/index constraints; snake_case tables and columns; `_at` for timestamps
(`timestamptz`), `_date` for dates. Constraints and indexes in the database, not only in code.
- Repositories: single-purpose methods named for the question (`findByEmail`, `listOverdueByCustomer`), no
  catch-all criteria object.
- Decide once per project, in DECISIONS.md, whether the ORM entity is the domain entity (default for CRUD-ish
  features) or maps to a pure domain entity (when real invariants exist).

**Monolith first.** One deployable API per product (plus the FastAPI process when Python is needed). Split out a
service only on a trigger recorded in DECISIONS.md (independent scaling, different runtime, separate deploy
cadence or team), and only for a feature that already talks through its facade/events.

**Not adopted by default** (only inside a genuinely complex feature, via DECISIONS.md): CQRS/command bus, a value
object for every primitive, separate domain and persistence models everywhere.

**Decisions:** a choice that is hard to reverse, surprising without context, or the result of a real trade-off
goes to DECISIONS.md (see `documentation.md`). Read existing decisions before proposing to change something
settled.

## 4. Style

- Enforced by tooling first (formatter + linter, §9); this section covers what tools can't check.
- Names say what things are in the domain's language: `approveOrder`, not `handleData`. Booleans read as
  questions (`isActive`, `hasAccess`). No abbreviations except universal ones (`id`, `url`).
- Small functions at one level of abstraction. Early returns over nested ifs.
- Strict typing: TypeScript `strict: true`, no `any` (use `unknown` + narrowing); Python type hints everywhere.
- Prefer plain functions and data over classes unless the framework wants classes (NestJS) or there is real state.
- Imports sorted, no unused code, no commented-out code (git remembers).
- Commits: Conventional Commits with scope, imperative, in the repo's language: `feat(orders): add approval by amount`.

## 5. Testing

Always use the best method for the risk, but **don't bury a medium project under thousands of tests.** Tests are
there to give confidence to change code, not to hit a number.

- **TDD for business logic and bugs:** write the failing test first, then the code. Every bug fix starts with a
  test that reproduces it.
- **Test behavior through public interfaces,** not implementation details. A refactor that doesn't change
  behavior shouldn't break tests.
- **Shape:** many fast unit tests on the domain; a few integration tests per feature on the real boundaries
  (DB, API); a handful of end-to-end tests for the critical user journeys only (login, checkout, the core flow).
- **Skip:** trivial getters/mappers, framework glue, snapshot-everything UI tests, tests that recompute the
  expected value the same way the code does.
- **Mock only what you don't own** (third-party APIs, email, payments). For your own DB prefer a real test
  database or a local stand-in.
- Never weaken, skip or delete a test to make it pass. If a test is wrong, say so and fix it deliberately.

## 6. Verification & self-review

**No "done" without fresh evidence.** Run it, read the output, then claim.

| Excuse | Reality |
|---|---|
| "Should work now" | Run the tests / the app. |
| "The linter passed" | Linter ≠ typecheck ≠ tests ≠ it works. Run the ones that apply. |
| "It's a small change" | Small changes break builds too. Run the checks. |
| "I'll test it at the end" | Run typecheck and the relevant tests while you go; full suite at the end. |
| "The test was flaky" | Prove it (rerun, read the failure) before dismissing it. |

Before closing, review your own diff (the `reviewer` subagent for larger changes, see `subagents.md`) against this checklist:
- Every change traces to the request; nothing out of scope slipped in.
- No file crossed 500 lines; responsibilities still single.
- Layers respected: no business logic in UI/controllers, no infrastructure in domain; architecture tests pass.
- Backend contract held (§3): cross-feature facade/events, error shape, pagination, idempotency.
- Errors handled at boundaries, inputs validated, no secrets, no leftover debug code.
- ARCHITECTURE.md still true (modules, public APIs, owned tables, integrations, key flows).
- Tests cover the new behavior and pass; no test was weakened.
- No speculative abstractions, no obvious comments, no dead code.

## 7. Debugging

- Root cause before fixing (`runner` reproduces and distills the failure, `explorer` traces the code path):
  reproduce, read the actual error and stack trace, form a hypothesis, test it.
- After **three failed fix attempts**, stop patching: the problem is likely in the design or in an assumption.
  Step back, re-read the whole code path, question your assumptions, and change approach. Only bring it to the
  user if a second, different approach also fails — and then with what you learned and a concrete proposal.
- Log the root cause and fix in the day log; if it's a trap others could fall into, add it to ARCHITECTURE.md
  under conventions/constraints.

## 8. Default stacks

For new projects (in existing ones, the repo's stack wins):

| Product | Stack | Read |
|---|---|---|
| Web application | Next.js (frontend) + NestJS (API) + PostgreSQL | `stacks/nextjs.md`, `stacks/nestjs.md` |
| Landing page / marketing site | Astro | `stacks/astro.md` |
| AI product | Next.js (frontend) + FastAPI (Python, AI/back) + PostgreSQL | `stacks/nextjs.md`, `stacks/fastapi.md` |

Read only the stack file(s) for the code you're touching.

## 9. Tooling: make the rules enforceable

A rule a tool can check should be checked by the tool. On a new project, set this up in the first task; on an
existing one, use what's there and list what's missing as a proposal in your final report.

- **Formatter + linter:** Prettier + ESLint (TS) / ruff format + ruff check (Python). Include `max-lines` (warn at
  500), no-explicit-any, unused-imports, import sorting.
- **Architecture tests:** a boundary rule no tool checks is a suggestion. Copy the tested templates from the
  skill's `templates/arch/` (paths match the stack layouts; each file says what it checks and how to install it):

  | Stack | Files | Command |
  |---|---|---|
  | Next.js | `nextjs/eslint-boundaries.config.mjs` + `nextjs/.dependency-cruiser.cjs` | `eslint` + `depcruise src` |
  | NestJS | `nestjs/.dependency-cruiser.cjs` + `nestjs/eslint-arch.config.mjs` | `depcruise src` + `eslint` |
  | FastAPI | `fastapi/importlinter.toml` (into `pyproject.toml`) | `lint-imports` |

  Not tool-checkable, so reviewed (the antagonist checks them): thin routes, data access only through the DAL,
  error shape, permission before existence, pagination, idempotency, async misuse.
- **Typecheck:** `tsc --noEmit` / pyright or mypy.
- **One verify command:** `npm run verify` (lint + typecheck + arch + test + build) or equivalent. Run it before
  claiming done.
- **CI** running the verify command on every push.

The `metodologia` skill also installs a post-edit hook that warns when an edited file passes 500 lines.

# Plan & execute The user wants you as independent as possible. The spec is the contract; inside it, you decide. Coming back with a question costs the user a context switch — only do it when a wrong guess would be expensive or irreversible. What makes autonomy safe is not asking more, it's **verifying more**: a clear pass/fail check defined before you start, evidence before you claim, and small committed steps you can roll back. ## 1. Plan Design with `references/engineering.md` (and the matching `references/stacks/*.md`) in mind. `python /scripts/bitacora.py req plan REQ-NNN` → creates `PLAN.md` next to the spec. Fill it: - **Approach:** the chosen design in a few lines. If you weighed real alternatives, log the choice in DECISIONS.md. - **Global constraints:** copy from the spec what every task must respect. - **Verification first:** the end-to-end check that proves the acceptance criteria — the exact command(s) or steps (tests, `npm run verify`, run the app and exercise the flow, a dry run of the process). Define it before writing code; it's your finish line. - **Tasks:** small steps (minutes, not hours) in dependency order, one line each, in the template's format: ``- [ ] T3 — · repo: backend · after: T1, T2 · verify: `npm test -- orders` · covers: R1, US-2``. `repo:` when the workspace has several, `after:` for dependencies, files (or for business work: deliverable/owner), how to verify it (a command inside backticks is machine-runnable — marathon mode runs it), and which requirements (R1, US-2…) it covers. Every requirement must be covered by some task. Group them in phases that each end in a green, committable state. Keep the plan short enough to read in two minutes. Set the spec's `status: planned`. ## 1b. The one gate: plan approval This is the single point where the user reviews — reading a 2-minute plan is far cheaper than reviewing hundreds of lines of code built on a wrong plan. Show the user, in Spanish, a compact version of the plan: - approach (2–3 lines), phases with their tasks (one line each), what's out of scope, the verification; - the key decisions/assumptions you're making; - the path to PLAN.md for the full version. Run `bitacora.py plan review REQ-NNN` first: it marks the plan `review` and prints the web URL, where the user can read the plan and press **Aprobar y lanzar ejecutor** or **Pedir cambios**. Give the URL along with the summary. Then wait for their decision, from whichever side it comes: - **In the chat** ("aprobado", "dale", "sí", or changes): record it with `bitacora.py plan approve REQ-NNN` (or `plan changes REQ-NNN --comments "..."`). - **On the web:** in Claude Code run `bitacora.py plan wait REQ-NNN` in the background to be notified; elsewhere, check `PLAN.md` status when the user says so. A web approval **already launched the executor** (status `launched`) — don't launch again; just log it. Web change requests are appended to PLAN.md's Progress log. Apply any changes and ask once more only if they changed the approach. Once approved, log the approval in today's log, and from there on **run autonomously to the end** (§2) — no further check-ins. Skip the gate only for Quick-track work (a change that fits in one sentence) or if the user said "hazlo directo". ## 1c. Run the approved plan: marathon, loop or goal **Marathon is the default for plans that will take days** (many tasks, or anything that won't finish in one sitting): an external supervisor runs one fresh headless session per task, with caps, stuck detection, usage-limit waits and reboot recovery — see `references/marathon.md`. Keep the **loop** (or Codex goal) for a plan of a few hours. Rule of thumb: more than ~8 tasks or "this will run overnight" → marathon. **From the HQ (planning room)** — the session runs inside the bitácora root (`~/bitacora`), the SessionStart context says HQ MODE: don't execute here. Set PLAN.md `status: approved`, then launch a separate executor session: ``` python /scripts/bitacora.py --project launch REQ-NNN [--mode marathon|loop] [--model haiku] [--agent codex] [--repo ] ``` From the web UI, the plan-approval form has a **Modo** select (Maratón, the default, or Loop) and launches it for you. Marathon runs with Haiku 5.5 + ultracode by default and escalates a failing task to Sonnet, then Opus (effort xhigh; `marathon.md` §Escalation ladder); control it from the req's **Maratón** tab or `bitacora.py --project

run-control REQ-NNN pause|resume|stop`. `launch` writes `HANDOFF.md` next to the plan (everything the executor needs), and opens a native terminal window (Linux terminal, macOS Terminal, or Windows Terminal) in the project's repo running Claude Code with `--dangerously-skip-permissions` and a self-paced `/loop` (or Codex with `--yolo` and `/goal`; or, in marathon mode, the supervisor, which starts each session with the same permission flags). Executor sessions always start with these flags — that's the user's rule; never launch one without them. The repo path is remembered per project (`/project.json`); pass `--repo` the first time or for a new project (the folder is created). Then log the launch in today's log, tell the user in one line, and stay available in the HQ for the next requirement. Default agent: Claude Code unless the user says Codex. **Inside the project repo** (no HQ), run the plan in this session: **Claude Code** (you have the `Skill` tool and a `loop` skill is listed): invoke the `loop` skill **without an interval** (self-paced), passing this prompt with the real paths filled in: ``` Execute the approved plan (REQ-NNN) following the metodologia skill, references/execution.md §2–§4. Each iteration: read PLAN.md (Progress log + unchecked tasks), take the next phase, implement it, run its verification, commit, tick the tasks and add a Progress log line. Record judgment calls under Rulings; don't ask the user. If a stop-and-ask item comes up (§2), work on everything independent of it, then ask once, batched, and stop the loop. When every task is ticked and the plan's Verification passes: do §4 (fresh-eyes review, statuses, bitácora, walkthrough, final report in Spanish) and stop the loop. ``` Do as much work as is sensible inside each iteration (a whole phase or more); the loop is there so the work survives long runs and resumes from PLAN.md, not to slow you down. Stop the loop yourself when the plan is done or blocked. If the `loop` skill isn't available, just execute the plan straight through in the current turn. **Codex**: use a goal. If you have a goal tool (`create_goal`), create the goal yourself with the text below; otherwise give the user this exact line to paste, and start working: ``` /goal Complete REQ-NNN by executing per the metodologia skill (references/execution.md) without stopping until every task is ticked, the plan's Verification passes with evidence, and the bitácora (today's log, PENDING, SUMMARY) is updated — or until a stop-and-ask item blocks progress. ``` The goal text is the stopping condition, so keep the verifiable end state in it. In Codex there are no bitácora hooks: at the start run `bitacora.py where` yourself and read SUMMARY/PENDING; before finishing, update the bitácora explicitly (the Stop hook won't remind you). **Other harnesses:** execute the plan straight through, using PLAN.md's Progress log as your checkpoint. ## 2. Execute - **One feature at a time.** Finish (verified, committed, logged) before starting the next; everything else waits in PENDING.md. - Work task by task. Tick `[x]` in PLAN.md and add a line to **Progress log** after each verified phase. PLAN.md is the handoff: if the context resets, it's how you (or the next session) pick up exactly where you left off. - **Keep your context clean with subagents** (`references/subagents.md`): `explorer` for code sweeps, `researcher` for docs and comparisons, `runner` for test suites/builds/logs. For long plans, an `implementer` per task — one at a time — then verify its result yourself before ticking the task. After each phase, `reviewer` ×2 (axes `spec` and `standards`) on the phase diff. Between unrelated pieces of work, or when the conversation gets very long, make sure PLAN.md and the bitácora are current and suggest a `/clear` to the user (one line, no waiting). - **Default: don't ask.** Library choice, naming, file layout, how to split a module, which test to write, how to handle an edge case the spec didn't cover: decide, record a ruling, move on. - **Rule conflict is an exception to that default.** If a user-controlled rule blocks the requested behavior, name the exact source and impact and ask whether the user wants a one-time exception or a permanent rule change before doing the blocked part. Pause only that part and continue independent work. Do not offer to change a higher-priority instruction this skill cannot edit; explain the constraint and an allowed alternative. See [`self-improvement.md`](self-improvement.md). - **Rulings, not stalls.** Record each judgment call under **Rulings** in PLAN.md: `what — why — cost if wrong`. The user reviews rulings afterwards instead of being interrupted. - **Stop and ask only for:** destroying data or work that can't be recovered (dropping tables, deleting files outside the repo, force-push, migrations on production data), actions visible outside the machine (push, deploy, publish, sending emails/messages, payments, spending money), credentials/security changes, or discovering the spec itself is wrong in a way that changes what gets built. Even then: batch the questions into one message and keep working on everything that doesn't depend on the answer. - **Scope discipline.** Improvements you notice outside the spec go to PENDING.md and to "Proposals" in your final report — not into the code, and not as an interruption. - **When an approach fails twice, don't pile on patches:** revert to the last green commit, rethink, update the plan, try a different approach. - Log significant decisions to DECISIONS.md *when they are made*, not at the end. ## 3. Git (solo developer) - If the repo is on `main`/`master`, create a short-lived branch per feature (`feat/`); in a repo with other active work, a worktree. - **Workspaces with several repos:** the same branch name in every repo the requirement touches; commit and verify per repo; keep cross-repo contracts (API shapes, shared types) in sync within the same phase; the branches are merged together, as one change. - **Before every commit, the antagonist gate** (`subagents.md` §The antagonist gate): it attacks the staged change, you triage — fix what's relevant now, defer the rest to PENDING.md with urgency/complexity — one review plus at most one re-review, never more. - Commit after every green phase (Conventional Commits, in the repo's language). Keep refactor commits separate from behavior commits. - **Cite IDs in commits** so the trace graph links code to the bitácora: a trailer line `Refs: REQ-012 T3` (add `D-004` / `P-007` when the commit implements a decision or closes a pending item). - `main` must stay deployable. Unfinished work that has to be merged goes behind a flag, off by default (and the flag removal goes to PENDING.md). - Don't merge the feature branch yourself: the user merges from the web UI's **Revisar** tab (one click merges every repo of the workspace together; "merge and publish" also pushes). **Push and deploy only after asking.** ## 4. Verify & close - Run the verification from the plan for real and read the output. "Should work" is not verification (see the excuse table in `engineering.md` §6). - **Fresh-eyes review:** for anything beyond a small change, the `reviewer` subagent ×2 (axes `spec` and `standards`) sees only the spec, PLAN.md and the diff and reports **only** correctness problems, unmet requirements and out-of-scope changes. Fix those; everything else goes to PENDING.md, not into the code — chasing every review nit is how over-engineering happens. - **Trace check:** `bitacora.py trace` must show no `uncovered` / `unknown-ref` / `dangling` issue for this REQ. - Update statuses (spec `in-progress` with what's missing, or leave it for the merge; plan `done`) and the bitácora (today's log, PENDING, SUMMARY; ARCHITECTURE if structure changed). - Write **`REPORT.md`** in the requirement folder (sections: Built, Verification evidence, Rulings, Needs your eyes, Proposals, Pending, Walkthrough). Update the relevant tests and instructions, preserve unrelated changes, and report actual verification. This standing authorization covers reversible skill-owned changes only: generated installed copies and machine-wide Codex/Claude settings are outside it unless the specific update is authorized. Ask before external, destructive, security-sensitive or unrelated system changes. A speculative idea is a proposal, not a change request. # Marathon mode

An external **supervisor** (`scripts/bt_run.py`) runs an approved PLAN for hours or days. It launches a **fresh
headless agent session per task**, keeps all state on disk, enforces the caps itself, detects stuck tasks, waits out
usage limits, survives reboots and notifies the user. Context never rots because every session starts clean; the
agent never has to "remember" anything — PLAN.md, RUN.json and the bitácora are the memory.

For a user asking for overnight or multi-day autonomous development, explain this mode and its resume/pause controls
before choosing it. Use [`agent-orchestration.md`](agent-orchestration.md) to decide task dependencies, worker
ownership, and verification. Marathon is a bounded execution mechanism: it does not authorize external or destructive
actions, permission bypass changes, or skipping the existing plan approval gate.

## Marathon vs loop

| | Loop / goal (`execution.md` §1c) | Marathon |
|---|---|---|
| Who drives | the agent itself, one long session | an external script, one session per task |
| Length | hours | days |
| Context | accumulates, needs `/clear` | clean for every task |
| Caps, stuck detection, usage-limit wait, reboot | none (manual) | built in |
| State | PLAN.md only | PLAN.md + `RUN.json` |

Default to marathon for plans with many tasks or that will outlast one sitting; keep the loop for a short plan you
expect to finish in a few hours. The decision also depends on whether each task can be expressed as a small,
independently verifiable unit; break down oversized tasks before launching.

## How it works

1. Plan approved (with **Modo: Maratón** on the web form, or via CLI). `launch --mode marathon` opens a native
   terminal window running the supervisor (Linux, macOS or Windows). The window stays visible: it prints one
   status line per session.
2. The supervisor creates/reads `RUN.json` (next to the spec, git-synced): task list parsed from PLAN.md, statuses,
   attempts, heartbeat, log of the last 200 sessions.
3. Loop: reload `RUN.json` (so controls are honored) → pick the next `todo` task whose `after:` dependencies are all
   done → build the session prompt → run ONE headless session with a hard timeout → classify the result → commit the
   bitácora → repeat.
4. When every task is done: a final session does the fresh-eyes review and writes `REPORT.md` (`execution.md` §4),
   then status `done`, PLAN `status: done`, notification, autostart removed.
5. If the only tasks left are blocked: status `blocked`, notification, exit.

The coordinator's plan remains the source of truth for scope and dependencies. The current supervisor dispatches one
task session at a time in dependency order. Parallelism within a task is appropriate only when the harness supports
it and ownership is disjoint. Each task session must return its status and evidence, while the supervisor's
verification decides whether `done` is accepted.

**Live session logs.** The agent writes straight into `.state/runs/<project>-<REQ>/session-0007.log` (machine-local)
while it runs, so `tail -f` shows it live and a killed or timed-out session still leaves its transcript. Claude runs
with `--output-format stream-json --verbose`: one JSON event per line (turns, tool calls, tool results) and a final
`result` event whose `is_error`, `result` and `total_cost_usd` the supervisor reads (the cost goes into the log
entry). Usage-limit detection reads that `result` event; when it never came, only the non-JSON lines (stderr) count,
so tool output in the transcript is never mistaken for a limit. Logs are capped at the last ~1 MB.

**Early termination.** `claude -p` can stay alive long after the agent finished (background jobs), and run into the
session timeout. While a session runs the supervisor polls RUN.json; once the agent has given its verdict for the
current task (`task done`, `task fail`, `task escalate`; for the final session, a fresh REPORT.md) it waits a 90 s
grace period (`BITACORA_RUN_GRACE_SEC` overrides it, for tests), then kills the session's process tree and settles
normally (verify, tick, log with `early_exit`; a `task fail` keeps the agent's reason, not "timeout"). If the agent
takes its verdict back (done, then fail) the grace starts over. Hence the prompt rule: the verdict is the **last**
command, after the day log and every commit, and nothing may be left running in the background.

### Task lines the supervisor parses

```
- [ ] T3 — <what> · repo: backend · after: T1, T2 · verify: `npm test -- orders` · covers: R1, US-2
- [ ] T4 — <design the sync protocol> · level: architecture · verify: `pytest tests/sync`
```

`repo:`, `after:`, `verify:` and `level:` are optional. `level: architecture` marks a hard architecture/design task:
it starts at the top of the escalation ladder (opus, effort xhigh) instead of haiku. `verify:` is run by the supervisor **only if it is inside backticks**
(from the task's repo dir, 10-minute timeout); free text is just guidance for the agent. Already-ticked `[x]` tasks
start as done. `repo`, `after`, `verify` and `level` are **frozen when the run starts**: later edits to PLAN.md (even by the
agent) are reported as plan drift and not adopted, so a session cannot rewrite its own gate; to change them, edit
RUN.json. New task lines are added. Write tasks small enough to finish in one session (minutes, not hours) and give each a machine-runnable
`verify` whenever possible: it is the supervisor's independent proof, the agent's claim alone is not trusted.

## What the session agent does (and must not do)

The session prompt carries the project/REQ/task (id, title, repo, verify), pointers (HANDOFF.md, SPEC.md, PLAN.md,
bitácora SUMMARY / ARCHITECTURE / TOOLS), a trace context bundle, the last log lines, notes and `last_error` for this
task, and the rules:

- Work **only on this task**. Follow `engineering.md` and run the antagonist gate before every commit.
- Commit on the feature branch. **Never push or deploy.**
- Finish with exactly one of:
  ```
  bitacora.py --project P task done REQ-001 T3 --evidence "<what proves it>"
  bitacora.py --project P task fail REQ-001 T3 --reason "<why>"
  ```
  `done` records the claim in RUN.json; the supervisor ticks the PLAN.md checkbox (and appends to the Progress log) only
  after its own `verify` passes. The session can only mark **its own task** (`task done|fail|note` for another id is
  rejected). `task fail REQ T --reason "..." --blocked` blocks the task at once. A note for the next attempt:
  `task note REQ-001 T3 --text "..."`.
- If the task turns out to be a hard architecture/design problem, or it can't find a solution, it does not flail:
  `task escalate REQ-001 T3 --to opus --reason "..."` (architecture) or `--to sonnet` (stuck), then stops (see
  the escalation ladder below).
- Wait for every workflow/subagent/background job it started before `task done`; leave nothing running.
- Log the session in the day log **before** the verdict: `task done|fail|escalate` is the last command (the
  supervisor ends the session shortly after it).

When `ultracode` is on (default) the prompt adds: *ultracode: use the Workflow tool for substantive multi-step work in
this task.*

## Caps, stuck tasks, usage limits

- **max_attempts** (default 4: haiku, sonnet, opus, opus) per task, **session_timeout_min** (default 60) per
  session, **max_sessions** (default 300) per run. Reaching max_sessions stops the run (status `stopped`) and
  notifies. A RUN.json created before the default changed keeps its own value.
- **Failed attempt** = timeout, the agent called `task fail`, the agent exited without marking `done`, or `done` but
  the backticked `verify` failed (`verify_failed`; the task goes back to `todo`). Every failed attempt moves the task
  **one tier up** the escalation ladder for its next session.
- **Escalated session** = the agent called `task escalate`: it counts toward max_attempts but is not a failure (no
  `error_hash`, never "same error twice").
- **Stuck** = attempts >= max_attempts, or the same normalized error (`error_hash`: numbers, paths and hex stripped)
  twice **with the second one already at the top tier** (opus); a repeated error below the top just escalates. The
  task becomes `blocked`, a PENDING item is added
  (`P-0xx · [blocked] REQ T: title — reason · urgency: high · … · marathon`), `pending_id` is set, the user is
  notified, and the run **continues with other tasks** that do not depend on it.
- **Usage / rate limit** (a **failed** session — non-zero exit or `is_error` — whose output mentions usage limit,
  rate limit, 429, quota, "try again at"…; a successful run that merely mentions them is not a limit): status
  `waiting`, `waiting_until` = now + backoff (30 min, doubling, max 4 h). It does **not** count as an attempt; one
  notification. The supervisor sleeps and retries by itself. After 8 limit results in a row on the same task, the
  next one is logged as `limit_streak`: it is **not an attempt and never a failure** (no `error_hash`, no "same
  error twice", no tier climb, `attempts` untouched), so limits alone never block a task or use up the ladder. It
  is counted in the task's `limit_streaks`, the supervisor waits after it like after any limit, and the user is
  notified on every streak (a misread failure that keeps looking like a limit can only be told apart by a human;
  `max_sessions` bounds it).
- **Done is a claim until verified.** Under the supervisor `task done` only sets `claimed_done` on the task (status
  stays `in_progress`); the task becomes `done`, and the PLAN.md box is ticked, once the supervisor's own `verify`
  passes. If the supervisor dies in between, the next start (`--resume`, autostart) re-runs the `verify` of every
  claimed-but-unverified task **before** picking new work (a failed verify is a normal failed attempt). A RUN.json
  from before this change, with a bare `done`, is trusted as it was.
- **Checkpoint is a resume hint, not fresh evidence.** On resume, load the approved plan and RUN.json, inspect the
  worktree and logs, and re-run each claimed task's verification before scheduling new work. Re-check any external
  fact, approval or environment assumption that may have changed since the checkpoint; never infer that a checkpoint
  authorizes an external side effect.
- **Supervisor errors** (RUN.json locked by git/antivirus, a missing file…) are logged, notified once, retried with a
  growing pause and only given up on after 10 in a row. A missing agent executable stops the run and notifies.

## Controls

| Action | Web (req tab **Maratón**) | CLI |
|---|---|---|
| Pause (after the current session) | Pausar | `bitacora.py --project P run-control REQ-001 pause` |
| Resume | Reanudar | `bitacora.py --project P run-control REQ-001 resume` |
| Stop | Detener | `bitacora.py --project P run-control REQ-001 stop` |

Controls write `control` into RUN.json; the supervisor polls it (paused: every 30 s). The tab also shows status,
progress x/y, current task, heartbeat age (a warning when older than session timeout + 10 min), `waiting_until`, the
task table and the last 30 log lines. The dashboard lists active marathons per project.

CLI to start by hand:

```
bitacora.py --project P run REQ-001 [--agent claude|codex] [--model haiku] [--no-ultracode]
    [--max-attempts 4] [--session-timeout 60] [--resume]
bitacora.py --project P launch REQ-001 --mode marathon --model haiku
```

`--agent-cmd "<template>"` (placeholders `{prompt_file} {workdir} {task} {req} {project} {model_args}`, the last one
being the tier's `--model … --effort …`) replaces the agent command;
it exists for tests only. `--once` runs a single session. `--retry-blocked` puts blocked tasks back to `todo` with
fresh attempts (use it after fixing the cause listed in PENDING.md). `--no-autostart` skips the per-user login entry.
`--resume` is accepted for readability but implicit: the supervisor always continues from RUN.json if it exists.
Codex receives its prompt on stdin (`exec ... -`) instead of as an argument; Claude takes it as the last argument.

## Remote monitoring (Remote Control)

Task sessions are headless, and Remote Control only attaches to interactive sessions — so a marathon launched with
Claude also opens a **monitor**: an interactive Haiku session named "`<project> <REQ> maratón`", started with
`claude --remote-control`, briefed by `MONITOR.md` (written next to the plan). The user opens it from claude.ai/code or
the Claude app and asks "¿cómo va?", "¿por qué se bloqueó T4?", "muéstrame el último commit", or "pausa / reanuda /
detén". The monitor reads RUN.json, the session logs, git and PENDING, and steers only through `run-control` and
`task note`; it never edits code. It is independent of the supervisor (closing it never stops the run) and idle
until asked.
- Open it again any time: `bitacora.py --project P monitor REQ-001`, or the web tab's **Abrir monitor remoto**.
- To start HQ sessions from the phone too, run `claude remote-control --name HQ` inside `~/bitacora`.

## Reboots and the stale heartbeat

On start the supervisor installs a per-user login entry that runs `run <REQ> --resume`:
Windows Startup `.cmd`, Linux systemd user service (XDG `.desktop` when systemd is absent), or
macOS `~/Library/LaunchAgents/*.plist`. POSIX entries resume headlessly; inspect RUN.json, logs or the web UI.
Entries take effect at the next login and are removed when the run ends as `done` or `stopped`.
The generated scripts preserve `BITACORA_ROOT` and the launch PATH. A Linux session without a user
systemd manager must support XDG Autostart or resume manually; errors are reported, not hidden. A restart continues from RUN.json, sends any
`in_progress` task back to `todo` (its session died with the machine), and **keeps an explicit pause and a pending
usage-limit wait** (only `run-control resume` lifts a pause). The heartbeat (`at`, `pid`, `machine`, `task`, `session`, `state`) is written
before and after every session: if it is stale the supervisor is dead — reopen it with `run REQ --resume`.

## Notifications

Native notifications (Windows toast, Linux notify-send, macOS osascript) on: blocked task, usage-limit wait, run done, run blocked, run stopped / cap reached.
Optional phone push through ntfy: create `.state/notify.json` with `{"ntfy_topic": "<secret-topic-name>"}` and
subscribe to that topic in the ntfy app. Notification failures are reported to stderr and never stop the run.

## Why Haiku 5.5 + ultracode

Marathon work is many small, well-specified tasks with an independent `verify`; a fast, cheap model burns far less of
the usage limit over days and the clean-session design removes its main weakness (long-context drift).
**ultracode** gives it the Workflow tool for the multi-step parts inside a task, and the verify + antagonist gate catch
its mistakes. A task that Haiku cannot finish climbs the escalation ladder instead of being retried blindly; only a
task that also fails at the top is blocked (with a PENDING item).

## Escalation ladder

| Tier | Claude | Codex |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | the run's `--model` (default **haiku**), default effort | its model, default effort |
| 1 | **sonnet** `--effort xhigh` | same model, `-c model_reasoning_effort="xhigh"` |
| 2 (top) | **opus** `--effort xhigh` | same model, `-c model_reasoning_effort="xhigh"` |

A configured model already stronger than a tier's (e.g. `--model opus`) is kept; only the effort rises. Codex never
switches model: from tier 1 up it only raises the reasoning effort.

- Each task keeps its `tier` (0–2) in RUN.json; each log entry records the `model` and `effort` of that session
  (the web tab shows both: the task table's **Modelo** column and the log's).
- **Up one tier** after every failed attempt (`failed`, `verify_failed`, `timeout`), capped at opus. A usage limit
  or a user stop does not move it.
- **Same error twice** below the top → escalate; at the top (opus) → `blocked`. With the default max_attempts 4 a
  task gets haiku, sonnet, opus, opus.
- **`level: architecture`** on the PLAN line → the task starts at tier 2 (opus xhigh).
- **`task escalate REQ T --to sonnet|opus --reason "..."`** (only for the session's own task) raises the tier, stores
  the reason in the task's notes so the next session reads it, and marks the session `escalated`. A target at or
  below the current tier is refused (the agent uses `task fail` instead), so an opus session cannot burn attempts
  "escalating" in place. Run by hand (no supervisor), it only changes the tier.
- `--retry-blocked` puts the task back at its starting tier (0, or 2 for `level: architecture`).
- The final review session climbs the same ladder with each failed attempt.

## Context care

- One task per session: the unit of work is sized so a clean session can finish it.
- On SessionStart (any source, especially after a compaction) the hook re-injects a **Current marathon task** block
  from `BITACORA_RUN` / `BITACORA_TASK`: REQ, task, verify, after, last_error, notes, and the rule *work only on this
  task; finish with task done/fail*.
- Noisy work (code sweeps, test suites, long logs) goes to subagents (`subagents.md`); the session keeps only
  conclusions.
- Notes for the next attempt go in `task note`, not in the agent's head: the next attempt is a different session.
